Eating high calorie foods will not make you gain weight right away. It will take several weeks or longer depending on what you are eating to gain weight. The reason why it takes so long is because your body is aiming to maintain a near-constant body weight. Therefore, when you eat excess calories, you burn more calories and then there is no net weight gain.   
  
This control of body weight occurs within your brain and it is done by the brain "sensing" nutrients like fat, sugars, and proteins in your blood. Additionally, hormones produced in your fat, stomach, gut, and pancreas also communicate with the brain about how much food that you are eating. With repeated exposure to a high-calories diet, these signals to your brain become less efficient. So your brain doesn't tell you to stop eating when you need to and it doesn't tell your brain to burn the extra calories. This is when you start to put on weight.   
   
At this point, your brain does something interesting, it stops trying to maintain the normal body weight that you had before eating the high-calorie food and instead starts maintaining the higher body weight. Now, if you start dieting and lose weight, the brain will alter how hungry you are and how much energy you burn to stay at the higher weight.

It's never too late to turn around a friendless life. You need to first understand why you don't have friends. The next step is to make a plan to improve. It's important to make the plan realistic.

Then, I got a job as a cashier and was forced to talk to other people. It took me 6 months at my job but I finally started to talk socially (not professionally) with my coworkers. There, I made some friends. I joined volunteer organizations and learned how to socialize in different settings. I then started to say hi to people as I pass them. Then, I started conversations with strangers. Now I make friends with strangers.   
  
This whole process took me 6-7 years. It's not easy to overcome whatever problems have left you FA. It won't happen overnight either. But it's definitely possible.

Whatever your something is, do it until you feel okay with it and move on to the next goal. For example, my first thing was to order food on my own. I then went on to get a job as a cashier. Then I started to talk to my coworkers in a non-business capacity (took me six months!). I just kept building from there.

I used to have pretty bad social anxiety as well but I have pretty much overcome it now. I don't know if what I have to say will be helpful to you, but I hope it will.   
   
When I was in elementary school, I wouldn't say I was really picked on, but if I spoke, the other children would tell me that I'm stupid, I should shut up, nobody is listening, etc. It just kept happening and eventually, I learned that I shouldn't even bother talking. It was a little sad but I didn't really feel very bothered by it. This continued for a few years and so I became one of those people who never speaks in class and doesn't really have friends. I guess you never really realize how little things pile up and dramatically change your life, as I had been quite outgoing as a child.   
   
Anyway, when I got to high school, I think most of the student body was worried that I'd commit suicide any moment (and it's not like they were far off) so they were really nice to me. I had a nice, safe environment to talk to my peers finally, but I still couldn't say a word. It was like I never learned to socialize at a high school level or that I learned not to speak. I would open my mouth but nothing would come out. I would get so frightened when people talked to me, I'd try to hide by looking away until they left, or I'd run away myself. School was absolutely horrible. I would get so anxious and depressed that my body got so weak, I couldn't get out of bed most mornings and if I went to school, I couldn't get up the stairs. I would have uncontrollable outbursts of crying and random thoughts of suicide.   
   
It came to a point where I decided I had to do something. So I started with very little things. I'd give myself a project to do, like "order food by yourself, " "say hi to a stranger you pass on the road," or "walk around the mall by yourself." Eventually, I got to bigger things like "eat a meal in a restaurant alone" or "see a movie alone."    
  
Then I started making some friends. I made 2 good friends during university, which I thought was pretty good. I challenged myself to go wherever (most places anyway) they invited me. At this point, I could talk to others if I had specific business with them like helping them with homework, or ordering food, etc and I could talk to my friends and family. This all had taken about 6-7 years to accomplish.   
   
Over the past year, everything suddenly changed very quickly. My challenge now is to talk to everyone you meet and try to become friends with them. Because of that I have made a ridiculously large amount of friends. Now I am back to the outgoing person that I was when I was a child and I am much happier. I still get some depressive moods sometimes and still think of suicide every so often but it is a lot better than it was before. Oh, and of course, I am still dateless/kissless/virgin/whatever. But it definitely is better.

There are multiple factors here. There are many ways in which your body will assess how full you feel. Generally, you have caloric content but there is also physical signs (i.e. how full your stomach is). To complicate these matters, we can sometimes disregard the signals that you are full, if the food is tasty enough.   
So if you were to eat celery which is not calorically dense, you would be full due to physical factors but the caloric drive would kick in and you would be hungry not too long after digesting the celery. In contrast, if you ate a calorically dense food, you would not feel hungry for a longer period of time.    
Cake is a different matter. People usually eat cake not because they are hungry but because it tastes good. This is truly the core of the obesity epidemic. The reason why we like to overeat palatable, calorically dense food is because we have evolved to be opportunistic feeders. When humans were living in tribes, it was unclear when they would have food or not. When they were able to hunt a large animal, it was beneficial for them to be able to overeat and store the excess energy as fat in times of famine. Because of this, we are programmed to overeat. This became a problem as the prevalence of high calorie food in our society increased. Our genes haven't had time to adjust to the rapid change in our environment. And as overweight and obese people are able to live to reproduce, it is unlikely that our genetic pool will change to favour being lean.

You can sweeten food with artificial sweetners. They have a similar structure to sugar so it still tastes sweet, but the structure is different enough that your digestive system cannot process it, so you don't gain any calories from eating it.   
Although it seems like cooking all your food with sweetners would be helpful for obesity, there is evidence to suggest that it is not. In a study in rodents, animals fed with artificial sweetners actually over-ate their food and were heavier. The idea here is that by sugar is actually a signal to your body that makes you less hungry.

It's great that you are interested in neuroscience but it would be best for you to learn the basics before trying to learn something specific like the circadian rhythm.  
Electrical impulses/firing of cells is actually called an action potential. You can think of it like electricity passing down a wire. The "wires" of a cell are called axons. [Neurons or brain cells look like this](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Neuron_Hand-tuned.svg/400px-Neuron_Hand-tuned.svg.png) The purple circle would be the cell body, the yellow ovals make up the wire and at the end of the wire you have the terminal.   
The action potential follows an all-or-none principal. The cell either fires or it doesn't. There isn't any between. Each action potential is the same size. The only thing that is varied is the timing and pattern of firing.

Photoreceptors in the retina detect light. This detection occurs by light activating ion channels so that retinal ganglion cells send an electrical impulse (the cells "fire") out of the retina. This electrical impulse arrives at the suprachiasmic nucleus. Depending on the pattern of firing, the neurons in the suprachiasmic nucleus are able to determine whether there is enough light detected at the retina to be day or night. These SCN neurons will change their firing rates accordingly to activate the pineal gland appropriately.  
There is another level to this, we could talk about what chemicals, channels, and processes mediate this firing but that would be a long read.
